category.title: Linked Lists & Memory Pointers
category.description: Singly, doubly, circular linked lists, pointer reversal, and cycle detection.

algorithms.title: Floyd's Cycle Detection (Tortoise and Hare Algorithm)
algorithms.summary: Detects cycles in a linked list or sequence using two pointers moving at different speeds (slow = 1 step, fast = 2 steps).
explanation: Initialize `slow` and `fast` pointers at head.
Move `slow` by 1 step (`slow = slow.next`) and `fast` by 2 steps (`fast = fast.next.next`).
If there is a cycle, `slow` and `fast` will eventually meet at the same node.
If `fast` reaches `null`, the list has no cycle.
To find cycle entry point: Reset `slow = head`. Move both `slow` and `fast` by 1 step. Their intersection point is the cycle start node.

traceSteps: Phase 1 (Detection): slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps.
Step 3: slow=-4, fast=-4 -> Collision at node -4! Cycle exists.
Phase 2 (Find Entry): Reset slow to head (3), keep fast at collision (-4). Move both 1 step at a time.
Step 1: slow=2, fast=2 -> Met at node 2!
Cycle starting node identified as node 2.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Detects presence of cycles and entry point in linked lists or pseudo-random generator sequences.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When asked if a linked list contains a loop or duplicate number in immutable array range [1, N].
wAnswers.whereUsed: Memory leak detection in circular references, deadlock detection in OS resource graphs, Pollard rho factorization.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Uses zero auxiliary memory O(1) space compared to Hash Set lookup which takes O(N) space.

algorithms.title: Linked List Paradigms: Iterative Pointer Rewiring vs Recursive Top-Down
algorithms.summary: Compares Iterative Pointer Manipulation (Bottom-Up forward traversal O(1) space) against Recursive Stack Rewiring (Top-Down unwinding).
explanation: Iterative Approach (Bottom-Up): Maintain pointers `prev`, `curr`, `next`. Traverse forward in O(1) space, updating `curr.next = prev` step by step.
Recursive Approach (Top-Down): Recurse to the last node first (`new_head = reverse(head.next)`).
During stack unwinding: set `head.next.next = head` and `head.next = None`.
Dummy Node Technique: Initialize `dummy = ListNode(0)` to handle edge cases where head node changes (e.g. deletion, insertion, merging).

traceSteps: Iterative: prev = None, curr = 1. next_node = 2. Set 1.next = None. prev = 1, curr = 2.
Step 2: curr = 2. next_node = 3. Set 2.next = 1. prev = 2, curr = 3.
Step 3: curr = 3. next_node = None. Set 3.next = 2. prev = 3, curr = None.
curr is None -> Loop ends. New head = prev = 3.
Recursive unwinding: Recurse 1->2->3. Base case at 3 returns head 3. Unwind at 2: 2.next.next=2 (3->2). Unwind at 1: 1.next.next=1 (2->1).
Both paradigms result in reversed list: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> None.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Mastery of pointer manipulation and recursive stack unwinding in sequential nodes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: Iterative for O(1) memory efficiency; Recursive for clean subproblem formulation.
wAnswers.whereUsed: LRU Cache doubly linked lists, OS kernel thread list scheduling, undo history buffers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) linear time pass over all nodes.

codeTemplates.code:
# Iterative O(1) Space
def reverse_iterative(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev

# Recursive Top-Down
def reverse_recursive(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_recursive(head.next)
    head.next.next = head
    head.next = None
    return new_head

algorithms.title: Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists (Iterative & Recursive)
algorithms.summary: Combines two sorted linked lists into a single sorted list by updating pointers in O(M+N) time.
explanation: Dummy Node Pattern: Create `dummy = ListNode(-1)` and `tail = dummy`.
Compare `l1.val` and `l2.val`.
If `l1.val <= l2.val`: attach `tail.next = l1` and advance `l1 = l1.next`.
Else: attach `tail.next = l2` and advance `l2 = l2.next`.
Advance `tail = tail.next`.
Attach remaining non-empty list (`tail.next = l1 if l1 else l2`) and return `dummy.next`.

traceSteps: Compare 1 vs 1: attach l1 (1), l1 moves to 2. List = -1 -> 1.
Compare 2 vs 1: attach l2 (1), l2 moves to 3. List = -1 -> 1 -> 1.
Compare 2 vs 3: attach l1 (2), l1 moves to 4. List = -1 -> 1 -> 1 -> 2.
Compare 4 vs 3: attach l2 (3), l2 moves to 4. List = -1 -> 1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3.
Compare 4 vs 4: attach l1 (4), l1 moves to None.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Combines 2 sorted linked sequences without instantiating new node memory.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When performing Merge Sort on linked lists or merging sorted data streams.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Merge Sort for linked lists, database external sort-merge join step.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(M + N) time with zero extra node memory allocated.

algorithms.title: Fast & Slow Pointer Pattern (Middle Finding & Cycle)
algorithms.summary: Uses two pointers moving at different speeds (slow by 1, fast by 2) to find the middle node or detect cycles in single pass.
explanation: Initialize `slow = head` and `fast = head`.
While `fast` is not None and `fast.next` is not None:
- Advance `slow = slow.next` (1 step).
- Advance `fast = fast.next.next` (2 steps).
When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` will be exactly at the middle node of the list!
For even-length lists: `slow` rests at second middle node.

traceSteps: Step 3: fast.next is None -> Loop terminates.
Middle Node = 3 found in a single pass O(N) time & O(1) space.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Locates the middle of a linked list or detects cycles in single-pass O(1) space.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When splitting a linked list into two equal halves (e.g. Merge Sort, Palindrome check).
wAnswers.whereUsed: Linked list merge sort partition, palindrome verification, cycle start detection.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N) single-pass with zero extra space.

algorithms.title: Remove N-th Node From End of List (Two-Pointer Gap)
algorithms.summary: Removes the N-th node from the end of a linked list in a single pass using a dummy node and a fixed-gap two-pointer technique.
explanation: Initialize `dummy` node pointing to `head` (handles head deletion edge case).
Set `first = dummy` and `second = dummy`.
Advance `first` pointer by `n + 1` steps to create a fixed gap of size `n` between `first` and `second`.
Move both `first` and `second` forward together until `first` reaches `None`.
Now `second` points to the node BEFORE the target node!
Perform deletion: `second.next = second.next.next` and return `dummy.next`.

traceSteps: Advance first by n+1 (3 steps): first = node 3.
first is None -> second rests at node 3 (node before 4).

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Deletes the N-th node from the end in single-pass O(1) auxiliary space.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding or modifying nodes relative to the end of a singly-linked list without storing length.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Buffer eviction algorithms, memory garbage collection, LRU list node removal.

algorithms.title: Merge Sort on Linked List (Top-Down Divide & Conquer O(N log N))
algorithms.summary: Sorts a linked list in O(N log N) time by finding the middle, splitting into two halves, recursively sorting both, and merging.
explanation: Base Case: If `head` is None or `head.next` is None, return `head`.
Divide: Find middle node using Fast & Slow pointers. Split list into `left` half and `right` half (`mid.next = None`).
Conquer: Recursively call `sortList(left)` and `sortList(right)`.
Combine: Merge the two sorted halves using `mergeTwoLists(left, right)` and return merged head.

traceSteps: Recursively sort left [4, 2]: split to [4] and [2] -> Merge returns [2, 4].
Recursively sort right [1, 3]: split to [1] and [3] -> Merge returns [1, 3].

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts a linked list in optimal O(N log N) time without needing random access array indices.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When sorting linked lists efficiently (preferred over Quick Sort due to no random access overhead).
wAnswers.whyOptimal: O(N log N) guaranteed worst-case sorting time.

algorithms.title: Singly Linked List Foundations & Operations
algorithms.summary: Linear node structure where each node holds data and a single forward pointer ('next') to the succeeding node.
explanation: A Singly Linked List consists of dynamically allocated nodes connected sequentially via 'next' pointers.
Head pointer stores the start of the list. Last node points to None/null.
Insertion/Deletion at Head takes O(1) time. Searching or accessing by index K takes O(K) time.
Reversing a Singly Linked List requires updating 'next' pointers in a single pass using prev, curr, and nxt pointers.

traceSteps: Reverse List: Iterate updating pointers: prev=None, curr=30.
Final Head points to 10: Head -> [10] -> [20] -> [30] -> None

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Provides dynamic size allocation without requiring contiguous physical memory allocation.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When frequent insertions and deletions at the head are needed without array resizing penalties.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Stack data structure implementation, hash table chaining for collision resolution, OS memory allocation blocks.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Avoids O(N) array element shifts during insertions and deletions.

algorithms.title: Doubly Linked List Foundations & Operations
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) Insertion & Deletion with direct node reference
algorithms.summary: Bi-directional node structure where each node holds data, a forward pointer ('next'), and a backward pointer ('prev').
explanation: A Doubly Linked List allows two-way traversal (forward and backward).
Each node has both `prev` and `next` pointers. Head's `prev` is None, and Tail's `next` is None.
Deletion of a specific node given its pointer takes O(1) time because `node.prev.next = node.next` and `node.next.prev = node.prev` directly access neighbors.
Reversing a Doubly Linked List is simplified by swapping `prev` and `next` pointers for every node.

exampleTrace.input: Insert 10, 20 into Doubly Linked List -> Delete node 10
traceSteps: Delete Node 10: 20.next updated to Null. Node 10 memory freed.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Allows O(1) deletion of given nodes and bidirectional linear traversal.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When backward traversal or fast removal of nodes from middle/tail is required.
wAnswers.whereUsed: LRU Cache (HashMap + Doubly Linked List), Browser history back/forward navigation, Music player queues.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Provides constant time O(1) removal of any node given its reference.

algorithms.title: Circular Singly Linked List
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(1) Insert at Head/Tail with Tail pointer, O(N) Traversal
algorithms.summary: Singly Linked List variant where the last node ('tail') points back to the first node ('head'), forming a closed loop.
explanation: In a Circular Singly Linked List, there is no Null termination. The last node's `next` pointer links back to `head`.
Maintaining a `tail` pointer allows O(1) insertions at both head (`tail.next`) and tail.
Traversal loops continuously until `curr == head` again.
Useful for round-robin scheduling algorithms where process loops continuously.

exampleTrace.input: Insert 10, 20 in Circular Singly Linked List
traceSteps: Insert 20 at tail: 20 added after 10. tail = [20]. 20.next = 10.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Eliminates null termination, allowing continuous cyclical traversal.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When resources or tasks need to be accessed continuously in a circular loop.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Operating System Round-Robin CPU scheduling, multiplayer board games (turn order), digital media playlists.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Seamless O(1) wrap-around from last element to first element without index reset code.

algorithms.title: Circular Doubly Linked List
algorithms.summary: Doubly Linked List variant where Head's `prev` points to Tail, and Tail's `next` points to Head, enabling instantaneous bidirectional loop navigation.
explanation: Combines advantages of Doubly Linked List and Circular Linked List.
`head.prev` directly gives `tail`, and `tail.next` directly gives `head` in O(1) time without keeping a separate tail variable.
Node insertion and deletion at both ends involve updating 4 pointer references (`prev` & `next` for adjacent nodes).
Extremely powerful structure for deque implementations and Fibonacci Heaps.

exampleTrace.input: Insert 10, 20 into Circular Doubly Linked List

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Enables O(1) bidirectional access to both ends of a circular list.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When both forward/backward continuous looping and fast O(1) head/tail modifications are needed.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Fibonacci Heap data structure, Advanced operating system kernel task schedulers, Undo-Redo circular ring buffers.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Provides constant time O(1) access to both ends without additional pointer overhead.

algorithms.title: Merge K Sorted Linked Lists
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N log K) where N is total nodes, K is number of lists
algorithms.summary: Merges K sorted linked lists into a single sorted linked list using a Min-Heap or Divide & Conquer approach.
explanation: Push the head node of all K lists into a Min-Heap Priority Queue.
Repeatedly pop the smallest node from the heap, attach it to the merged list, and push its `next` node into the heap.
Alternatively, merge lists pairwise using Divide & Conquer (merge 2 lists at a time).
Achieves optimal O(N log K) time complexity.

traceSteps: Push initial heads (1 from L1, 1 from L2, 2 from L3) into Min-Heap.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Combines K sorted streams or linked lists into one unified sorted sequence efficiently.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When merging multiple sorted logs, database partitions, or sorted linked list chains.
wAnswers.whereUsed: External merge sort in database engines, distributed log aggregation engines.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Min-heap maintains logarithmic selection O(log K) for each of the N total nodes.

algorithms.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N + M) where N, M are lengths of the two lists
algorithms.summary: Finds the node at which two singly linked lists intersect using two pointer traversal.
explanation: Initialize pointer `pA` at headA and pointer `pB` at headB.
Traverse both lists. When `pA` reaches the end of list A, redirect it to headB.
When `pB` reaches the end of list B, redirect it to headA.
If the lists intersect, `pA` and `pB` will meet at the intersection node after traversing (LenA + LenB) steps.
If no intersection exists, both pointers will equal Null simultaneously.

exampleTrace.input: List A: [4, 1, 8, 4, 5], List B: [5, 6, 1, 8, 4, 5], Intersect at node 8
traceSteps: Advance both pointers. pA reaches end of A first, redirects to 5 (headB).
pB reaches end of B, redirects to 4 (headA).
Both pointers are now synchronized in distance to the intersection point!
pA and pB advance simultaneously and meet at node 8. Return node 8.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the exact memory junction node shared by two merging linked list paths.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When detecting shared memory nodes or merged execution graphs without modifying data.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Garbage collector reference counts, git commit branch merge base identification.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Requires zero extra space O(1) and exact single pass O(N+M).

codeTemplates.code:
def getIntersectionNode(headA: ListNode, headB: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    if not headA or not headB: return None
    pA, pB = headA, headB
    while pA != pB:
        pA = pA.next if pA else headB
        pB = pB.next if pB else headA
    return pA

algorithms.title: Flatten a Multilevel Linked List
algorithms.timeComplexity: O(N) where N is total nodes across all levels
algorithms.spaceComplexity: O(N) for recursion stack or O(1) iterative pointer modification
algorithms.summary: Flattens a 2D or multilevel linked list with `child` pointers into a single-level doubly/singly linked list.
explanation: Iterate through nodes. When a node has a `child` pointer:
Find the tail node of the child list.
Connect child tail's `next` pointer to `curr.next`.
Connect `curr.next` to `curr.child` and set `curr.child = None`.
Continue iterating until all levels are flattened into 1D.

traceSteps: Iterate curr to Node 3. Detect child Node 7.
Find tail of child list: Node 8.
Connect Node 3.next to Node 7 and clear child pointer.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Transforms hierarchical 2D node graphs into a linear sequence.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When unnesting recursive linked structures into a single continuous stream.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Document tree flattening, DOM element sequence linearization, compiler AST unrolling.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Linear O(N) traversal without duplicating node data.

codeTemplates.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, prev=None, next=None, child=None):
        self.val = val
        self.prev = prev
        self.next = next
        self.child = child

def flatten(head: 'Node') -> 'Node':
    if not head: return None
    curr = head
    while curr:
        if curr.child:
            nxt = curr.next
            child_tail = curr.child
            while child_tail.next:
                child_tail = child_tail.next
            child_tail.next = nxt
            if nxt: nxt.prev = child_tail
            curr.next = curr.child
            curr.child.prev = curr
            curr.child = None
        curr = curr.next
    return head

algorithms.title: Clone Linked List with Random Pointer
algorithms.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra space using node interleaving (or O(N) using HashMap)
algorithms.summary: Creates a deep copy of a linked list where each node contains an extra `random` pointer referencing any node or Null.
explanation: Method (Interleaving):
Step 1: Create copied node A' right after original node A (A -> A' -> B -> B').
Step 2: Assign random pointers: `curr.next.random = curr.random.next` if `curr.random` exists.
Step 3: Separate original list and cloned list by updating `next` pointers.
Returns head of deep cloned list in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

exampleTrace.output: Cloned independent copies of 7 and 13 with random pointers intact
traceSteps: Step 3 (Separate): Extract [7', 13'] into independent cloned list.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Deep copies complex graph/linked-list structures containing arbitrary reference pointers.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When cloning memory structures with arbitrary pointers without modifying originals.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Object graph serialization, deep copy state cloning, virtual machine heap duplication.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Interleaving nodes avoids O(N) extra hash map memory overhead.

codeTemplates.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, x: int, next: 'Node' = None, random: 'Node' = None):
        self.val = int(x)
        self.next = next
        self.random = random

def copyRandomList(head: 'Node') -> 'Node':
    if not head: return None
    
    # Step 1: Interleave cloned nodes
    curr = head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        copy = Node(curr.val, nxt)
        curr.next = copy
        curr = nxt
        
    # Step 2: Assign random pointers
    curr = head
    while curr:
        if curr.random:
            curr.next.random = curr.random.next
        curr = curr.next.next
        
    # Step 3: Separate lists
    curr = head
    dummy = Node(0)
    copy_curr = dummy
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next.next
        copy = curr.next
        copy_curr.next = copy
        copy_curr = copy
        curr.next = nxt
        curr = nxt
        
    return dummy.next

algorithms.title: Palindrome Linked List
algorithms.summary: Checks if a singly linked list is a palindrome in O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
explanation: Step 1: Find the middle of the linked list using Fast & Slow pointers.
Step 2: Reverse the second half of the linked list in-place.
Step 3: Compare values of the first half and reversed second half node-by-node.
Step 4: (Optional) Restore the original list structure by re-reversing the second half.
Returns True if symmetric, False otherwise.

traceSteps: Find middle using fast/slow pointer: slow points to 2nd '2'.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Determines whether node values form a palindrome without extra array memory.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When checking symmetry in linked structures with strict O(1) space constraint.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Bioinformatics DNA sequence symmetry checks, text processing queues.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reversing second half in-place achieves linear O(N) time with zero extra space O(1).

codeTemplates.code:
def isPalindrome(head: ListNode) -> bool:
    if not head or not head.next: return True
    
    # Step 1: Find middle
    slow, fast = head, head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        
    # Step 2: Reverse second half
    prev = None
    curr = slow
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
        
    # Step 3: Compare halves
    first, second = head, prev
    while second:
        if first.val != second.val:
            return False
        first = first.next
        second = second.next
        
    return True

algorithms.title: Sort Linked List (Merge Sort O(N log N))
algorithms.spaceComplexity: O(log N) recursion stack space (or O(1) iterative bottom-up)
algorithms.summary: Sorts a linked list in O(N log N) time using Top-Down or Bottom-Up Merge Sort.
explanation: Split list into two halves using Fast & Slow pointer middle finding.
Recursively sort left and right sublists.
Merge two sorted sublists together using standard two-pointer merge algorithm.
Optimal sorting algorithm for linked list memory structures.

traceSteps: Split list at middle: Left [4, 2], Right [1, 3].
Merge [2, 4] and [1, 3]: Compare 2 & 1 -> append 1. Compare 2 & 3 -> append 2. Compare 4 & 3 -> append 3. Append remaining 4.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Sorts linked list nodes efficiently without converting to array.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When sorting linked lists in guaranteed O(N log N) time.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Sorting external dynamic memory lists, kernel task priority sorting.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Merge Sort is ideal for Linked Lists because elements can be re-linked in O(1) auxiliary space.

codeTemplates.code:
def sortList(head: ListNode) -> ListNode:
    if not head or not head.next: return head
    
    # Find middle (slow will point to node before mid)
    slow, fast = head, head.next
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        
    mid = slow.next
    slow.next = None  # Cut list
    
    left = sortList(head)
    right = sortList(mid)
    
    # Merge sorted lists
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    curr = dummy
    while left and right:
        if left.val < right.val:
            curr.next = left
            left = left.next
        else:
            curr.next = right
            right = right.next
        curr = curr.next
    curr.next = left or right
    return dummy.next
